<!-- site: execute -->

Use this guide if you work with Stephen Mildenhall's package
[`aggregate`](https://aggregate.readthedocs.io/) and want the same work in
prospicio from R. It also teaches the collective risk model to readers new to
both. It follows the "`aggregate` in Twenty Minutes" session (release 1.2.0)
step by step, with the published numbers beside prospicio's. Where the two
differ, the cause is a convention.

This is the R twin of the Python guide [`prospicio-for-aggregate-users.md`](prospicio-for-aggregate-users.md), with the same sections, models and numbers.

Money is in the units of that session (think thousands).
`R/prospicio/tests/test-guides.R` checks every printed number. To render the page, install the
R package (`remotes::install_github`, see `R/prospicio/bootstrap.R`) and run
`quarto render docs/guides/prospicio-for-aggregate-users.qmd`.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(prospicio)
```

## 1. The idea, and what is different

Both libraries compute the distribution of the total loss of a year,
`S = X_1 + ... + X_N`. They discretize the severity onto a grid, apply the
probability generating function of the count with a fast Fourier transform
(FFT), and read everything off the resulting probabilities. They differ in how
you ask:

| | `aggregate` | prospicio (R) |
|---|---|---|
| Model written as | a DecL program (a string): `agg Casualty 250 claims 1000 xs 0 sev lognorm 100 cv 1.5 poisson` | R objects: a count, a severity, a grid |
| Grid | chosen for you (`bs`, `log2`), overridable with `hints{}` | `compound_auto()` sizes it for an unlimited severity. With a limit, a layer or a portfolio you give the step and the number of points. `audit_grid()` re-runs the build around it as `sharpen` does |
| Result | an `Aggregate` object holding DataFrames | a `grid_distribution` (the distribution) whose `report` holds the checks |
| Reinsurance | clauses in the program (`occurrence net of ...`) | `xol_layer()` and `reinsurance_tower()` applied to the grid with `tower_on_grid()` |

Two habits carry over unchanged. **Validate the gross distribution before you
reinsure it**: the closed form you validate against disappears once you apply a
cover. And **an FFT answer is deterministic**: the same inputs give the same
digits every run.

The rest of this guide is the tour. Section 12 collects the DecL clauses in one
table. Section 13 gives timings and the grid audit.

## 2. Exact and discrete: the dice

`aggregate`'s first example is `agg Eg1 dfreq [1:5] dsev [1:3]`: a count of 1 to
5 and a severity of 1 to 3, all equally likely. In prospicio an empirical count
is `empirical_count()` (probabilities for 0, 1, 2, ...) and an empirical
severity is a `grid_distribution()` with step 1. `compound_distribution()`
compounds them. Its default method is Panjer's recursion, so ask for the FFT. R
indexes from 1, so the probability of a total of `k` is `probs[k + 1]`.

```{r}
count <- empirical_count(c(0, rep(1 / 5, 5)))
severity <- grid_distribution(1, c(0, rep(1 / 3, 3)))
eg1 <- compound_distribution(count, severity, 16, method = "fft")
cat(sprintf("mean %.4f, sd %.4f\n", mean(eg1), sqrt(variance(eg1))))
cat(sprintf("pmf(1) %.6f = 1/15, pmf(15) %.8f = 1/1215\n", eg1@probs[2], eg1@probs[16]))
cat(sprintf("cdf(5) %.6f\n", cdf(eg1, 5)))
```

```text
mean 6.0000, sd 3.1623
pmf(1) 0.066667 = 1/15, pmf(15) 0.00082305 = 1/1215
cdf(5) 0.465021
```

Every bar is an exact probability.

```{r}
#| label: dice-figure
library(ggplot2, exclude = "layer")   # keeps prospicio's layer()
ggplot(data.frame(total = 1:15, probability = eg1@probs[2:16]), aes(total, probability)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "total of the year (claim units)", y = "probability",
       title = "Eg1: the total of 1 to 5 claims of size 1 to 3")
```

The smallest outcome is one claim of size one, `1/5 * 1/3`. The largest is five
claims of size three, `1/5 * (1/3)^5`. The grid returns both exactly. The method
is exact for a discrete severity on a grid, so there is nothing to validate.

## 3. The casualty book

The main example of the session is a book of 250 claims. The severity is
lognormal with mean 100 and coefficient of variation (CV) 1.5, and each claim
has a limit of 1,000:

```
agg Casualty 250 claims 1000 xs 0 sev lognorm 100 cv 1.5 poisson
```

In prospicio this is a few lines. `discretize()` puts the severity on a grid.
The limit is a mapping on the grid (`map_grid()` keeps the mean exactly). The
count is a `poisson_count()`, and `compound_distribution()` compounds them. The
step of 1 and `2^16` points are what `aggregate` uses for this book.

```{r}
library(gt)

STEP <- 1
POINTS <- 2^16

# The severity capped at limit, on a grid: `limit xs 0`.
limited_severity <- function(severity, limit, step = STEP, points = POINTS) {
  grid <- discretize(severity, step, points, method = "local_moment")
  map_grid(grid, function(x) min(x, limit))$grid
}

# A table of list(label, prospicio, book, decimals[, book decimals]) rows; a NULL book value stays blank.
compare <- function(rows, title, subtitle) {
  frame <- data.frame(
    measure = vapply(rows, function(r) r[[1]], ""),
    prospicio = vapply(rows, function(r) as.numeric(r[[2]]), 0),
    book = vapply(rows, function(r) if (is.null(r[[3]])) NA_real_ else as.numeric(r[[3]]), 0)
  )
  table <- gt(frame, rowname_col = "measure")
  for (i in seq_along(rows)) {
    r <- rows[[i]]
    table <- table |>
      fmt_number(columns = "prospicio", rows = i, decimals = r[[4]]) |>
      fmt_number(columns = "book", rows = i, decimals = if (length(r) > 4) r[[5]] else r[[4]])
  }
  table |> sub_missing(missing_text = "") |> tab_header(title, subtitle)
}

claim <- limited_severity(lognormal_from_mean_cv(100, 1.5), 1000)
casualty <- compound_distribution(poisson_count(250), claim, POINTS, method = "fft")
p <- c(0.01, 0.5, 0.99, 0.999)
q <- unname(quantile(casualty, p))
compare(
  list(
    list("claim mean", mean(claim), 98.137, 3),
    list("annual mean", mean(casualty), 24534, 1, 0),
    list("annual sd", sqrt(variance(casualty)), 2561.7, 1),
    list("1% quantile", q[1], 18954, 0),
    list("median", q[2], 24449, 0),
    list("99% quantile", q[3], 30862, 0),
    list("99.9% quantile", q[4], 33169, 0)
  ),
  "The casualty book against aggregate 1.2.0", "Claim units"
)
```

```text
                prospicio     book
claim mean         98.137   98.137
annual mean      24,534.1   24,534
annual sd         2,561.7  2,561.7
1% quantile        18,954   18,954
median             24,449   24,449
99% quantile       30,862   30,862
99.9% quantile     33,170   33,169
```

The two agree to the digits shown, except the 99.9% quantile (section 9).

```{r}
#| label: casualty-figure
xs <- 15000:36000
top <- max(casualty@probs[xs + 1])
marks <- data.frame(q = quantile(casualty, p), label = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * p),
                    y = ifelse(p == 0.5, 0.05, 0.35) * top)
ggplot(data.frame(loss = xs, probability = casualty@probs[xs + 1]), aes(loss, probability)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = marks$q, colour = "grey50", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_text(aes(q, y, label = label), data = marks, hjust = -0.1, colour = "grey40",
            inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "annual loss", y = "probability per unit of loss",
       title = "The casualty book: distribution of the annual total")
```

## 4. A vocabulary of severities

`aggregate` takes any `scipy.stats` family by mean and CV, and it takes mixtures
by weights. The continuous families of prospicio have R constructors
(`lognormal()`, `gamma_distribution()`, `weibull_distribution()`, `pareto()`,
`burr_distribution()` and others, with `lognormal_from_mean_cv()` and
`gamma_from_mean_cv()` by mean and CV). A mixture of limited severities is the
weighted sum of their grids. The session's three-component book,

```
agg Mix 100 claims 2000 xs 0 sev lognorm [50 100 200] cv [1 1.5 2] wts [.5 .3 .2] poisson
```

is a weighted average of three limited, discretized lognormals:

```{r}
# A mixture of limited severities, from weights and severities.
mixed_severity <- function(weights, severities, limit, step = STEP, points = POINTS) {
  probs <- numeric(points)
  for (i in seq_along(weights)) {
    p <- limited_severity(severities[[i]], limit, step, points)@probs # ends at the limit
    probs[seq_along(p)] <- probs[seq_along(p)] + weights[i] * p
  }
  grid_distribution(step, probs)
}

mix_claim <- mixed_severity(
  c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2),
  list(
    lognormal_from_mean_cv(50, 1.0),
    lognormal_from_mean_cv(100, 1.5),
    lognormal_from_mean_cv(200, 2.0)
  ),
  2000
)
mix <- compound_distribution(poisson_count(100), mix_claim, POINTS, method = "fft")
mq <- unname(quantile(mix, c(0.01, 0.5, 0.99)))
compare(
  list(
    list("claim mean", mean(mix_claim), 92.996, 3),
    list("annual mean", mean(mix), 9299.6, 1),
    list("annual sd", sqrt(variance(mix)), 1894.5, 1),
    list("1% quantile", mq[1], 5638, 0),
    list("median", mq[2], 9130, 0),
    list("99% quantile", mq[3], 14423, 0)
  ),
  "The three-component book against aggregate 1.2.0", "Claim units"
)
```

```text
              prospicio     book
claim mean       92.996   92.996
annual mean     9,299.6  9,299.6
annual sd       1,894.5  1,894.5
1% quantile       5,638    5,638
median            9,130    9,130
99% quantile     14,423   14,423
```

Tail shape has a visible price. Two books with the same mean and CV differ at the 99.9% level:

```{r}
families <- list(
  lognormal = lognormal_from_mean_cv(100, 2),
  gamma = gamma_from_mean_cv(100, 2)
)
published <- c(lognormal = 13980, gamma = 11166)
tails <- list()
for (name in names(families)) {
  tail_book <- compound_distribution(
    poisson_count(50), limited_severity(families[[name]], 20000), POINTS, method = "fft"
  )
  tails <- c(tails, list(
    list(paste0(name, ", mean"), mean(tail_book), NULL, 0),
    list(paste0(name, ", 99.9%"), quantile(tail_book, 0.999), published[[name]], 0)
  ))
}
compare(tails, "Same mean and CV, different tail", "50 claims, CV 2; claim units")
```

```text
                  prospicio    book
lognormal, mean       5,000
lognormal, 99.9%     13,979  13,980
gamma, mean           5,000
gamma, 99.9%         11,166  11,166
```

The digits can differ by the cap, but the ordering is the point: the
lognormal's 99.9% sits well above the gamma's.

## 5. Frequency: Poisson is an opinion

A Poisson count says that years differ only by chance. Years can also differ for
reasons that all claims share (weather, inflation, the legal climate). Then the
count is over-dispersed. `mixed gamma 0.4` in DecL multiplies the Poisson rate
by a gamma factor of mean 1 and CV 0.4. In prospicio it is
`mixed_poisson_count()`:

```{r}
book <- limited_severity(lognormal_from_mean_cv(100, 1.5), 1000)
poisson <- compound_distribution(poisson_count(100), book, POINTS, method = "fft")
mixed <- compound_distribution(mixed_poisson_count(100, 0.4), book, POINTS, method = "fft")
agg_cv <- function(g) sqrt(variance(g)) / mean(g)
frame <- data.frame(
  measure = c("agg CV", "agg CV, book", "99.5% VaR", "99.5% VaR, book"),
  Poisson = c(agg_cv(poisson), 0.165, quantile(poisson, 0.995), 14456),
  `mixed gamma` = c(agg_cv(mixed), 0.433, quantile(mixed, 0.995), 23914),
  check.names = FALSE
)
gt(frame, rowname_col = "measure") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c("Poisson", "mixed gamma"), rows = 1:2, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c("Poisson", "mixed gamma"), rows = 3:4, decimals = 0) |>
  tab_header("Poisson against mixed gamma count", "Annual loss in claim units")
```

```text
                 Poisson  mixed gamma
agg CV             0.165        0.433
agg CV, book       0.165        0.433
99.5% VaR         14,456       23,914
99.5% VaR, book   14,456       23,914
```

The mixed count has the same mean, and its capital is about two-thirds higher.

```{r}
#| label: mixed-figure
xs <- 0:40000
both <- data.frame(
  loss = rep(xs, 2),
  probability = c(poisson@probs[xs + 1], mixed@probs[xs + 1]),
  count = factor(rep(c("Poisson", "mixed gamma"), each = length(xs)),
                 levels = c("Poisson", "mixed gamma"))
)
ggplot(both, aes(loss, probability, colour = count)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "annual loss", y = "probability per unit of loss", colour = NULL,
       title = "Poisson against mixed gamma count: same mean, longer tail") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Other mixing families, zero-modified and zero-truncated counts and the
logarithmic are count constructors too (`zero_truncated_count()`,
`zero_modified_count()`, `logarithmic_count()`, and `mixed_poisson_count()` with
`mixing = "inverse_gaussian"`). The Python guide
[Severity and frequency](severity-and-frequency.md) explains when to use which.

## 6. Trust, but verify

`aggregate` validates (the V in Mildenhall's SUVA-use cycle) by comparing moments computed exactly from the specification with moments estimated from the FFT output. The grid of prospicio carries the same audit in its `report` property. The closed form:

```{r}
n <- 250
exact_mean <- n * mean(claim)
exact_var <- n * (variance(claim) + mean(claim)^2) # Poisson: n * E[X^2]
report <- casualty@report
cat(sprintf("mean: exact %.4f, grid %.4f\n", exact_mean, mean(casualty)))
cat(sprintf("variance: exact %.1f, grid %.1f\n", exact_var, variance(casualty)))
cat(sprintf("aliasing error below 1e-15: %s, tail mass %.1e\n",
            report$aliasing_error < 1e-15, report$tail_mass))
```

```text
mean: exact 24534.1289, grid 24534.1289
variance: exact 6562423.0, grid 6562423.0
aliasing error below 1e-15: TRUE, tail mass 0.0e+00
```

For a continuous severity, the gap is discretization error, which the step
controls. The aliasing error shows whether the FFT buffer was long enough. The
tail mass is the probability that fell off the end of the grid. Read both every
time, as the Python guide [Aggregate distributions](aggregate-distributions.md)
explains. Here the aliasing error is rounding noise, below `1e-18`. Its digits
change with the platform, so the check prints only that it is small.

## 7. Limits, attachments and increased limits factors

Policy terms are a mapping on the grid, and increased limits factors are a loop over the limit (the session's `100 claims lim xs 0 sev lognorm 100 cv 1.5`):

```{r}
base_grid <- discretize(lognormal_from_mean_cv(100, 1.5), STEP, POINTS, method = "local_moment")
limits <- c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000)
means <- vapply(limits, function(limit) {
  capped <- map_grid(base_grid, function(x) min(x, limit))$grid
  mean(compound_distribution(poisson_count(100), capped, POINTS, method = "fft"))
}, 0)
ilf <- data.frame(
  limit = formatC(limits, format = "d", big.mark = ","),
  `E[S]` = means,
  `E[S], book` = c(9334, 9814, 9963, 9997),
  ILF = means / means[1],
  `ILF, book` = c(1.000, 1.051, 1.067, 1.071),
  check.names = FALSE
)
gt(ilf, rowname_col = "limit") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c("E[S]", "E[S], book"), decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c("ILF", "ILF, book"), decimals = 3) |>
  tab_header("Increased limits factors", "100 claims, lognormal severity, mean 100 and CV 1.5")
```

```text
        E[S]  E[S], book    ILF  ILF, book
500    9,334       9,334  1.000      1.000
1,000  9,814       9,814  1.051      1.051
2,000  9,963       9,963  1.067      1.067
5,000  9,997       9,997  1.071      1.071
```

A layer that attaches above zero, `300 xs 200`, has two readings in DecL. The
default is the severity conditional on exceeding the attachment, with the claim
count thinned by the probability of exceeding it. A trailing `!` keeps every
claim, most of them paying nothing. For a Poisson count the two give the same
annual distribution, because thinning a Poisson count gives a Poisson count with
a smaller mean. prospicio takes the second route and keeps the full count. The
check builds the first route by hand:

```{r}
full <- discretize(lognormal_from_mean_cv(100, 1.5), STEP, POINTS, method = "local_moment")
layered <- map_grid(full, function(x) min(max(x - 200, 0), 300))$grid # 300 xs 200
p0 <- layered@probs[1]
conditional <- grid_distribution(STEP, c(0, layered@probs[-1] / (1 - p0)))
unconditional <- compound_distribution(poisson_count(40), layered, POINTS, method = "fft")
thinned <- compound_distribution(poisson_count(40 * (1 - p0)), conditional, POINTS, method = "fft")
cat(sprintf("claims reaching the layer: %.3f of 40\n", 40 * (1 - p0)))
cat(sprintf("mean %.4f vs %.4f\n", mean(unconditional), mean(thinned)))
cat(sprintf("99%% %.0f vs %.0f\n", quantile(unconditional, 0.99), quantile(thinned, 0.99)))
```

```text
claims reaching the layer: 4.732 of 40
mean 631.2392 vs 631.2392
99% 1663 vs 1663
```

A binomial or fixed count is not closed under thinning. With such a count the
two readings differ, and the conditional one needs the thinned count.

## 8. Reinsurance, gross to net

The `Book` of the session has ten claims limited to 1,000, with lognormal
severity of mean 100 and CV 2. A reinsurer takes half of 300 xs 200 and all of
500 xs 500 per occurrence:

```
agg Book 10 claims 1000 xs 0 sev lognorm 100 cv 2
    occurrence net of 50% po 300 xs 200 and 100% po 500 xs 500 poisson
```

An `xol_layer()` is a limit, an attachment and a placed share. A
`reinsurance_tower()` holds the layers. `tower_on_grid()` applies them to the
grid. It returns the ceded loss of each layer and, when there are no annual
terms, the net.

```{r}
book_claim <- limited_severity(lognormal_from_mean_cv(100, 2), 1000, STEP, 2^14)
programme <- reinsurance_tower(list(
  xol_layer("half of 300 xs 200", 300, 200, share = 0.5),
  xol_layer("500 xs 500", 500, 500)
))
cover <- tower_on_grid(programme, poisson_count(10), book_claim, 2^14)
gross <- compound_distribution(poisson_count(10), book_claim, 2^14, method = "fft")
ceded_mean <- sum(vapply(cover$ceded, mean, numeric(1)))
layer_mean <- vapply(cover$ceded, mean, 0)
layer_sd <- vapply(cover$ceded, function(g) sqrt(variance(g)), 0)
tower <- data.frame(
  view = c("gross", names(cover$ceded), "ceded, both layers", "net"),
  mean = c(mean(gross), layer_mean, ceded_mean, mean(cover$net)),
  `mean, book` = c(952.7, NA, NA, 161.52, 791.18),
  sd = c(NA, layer_sd, NA, sqrt(variance(cover$net))),
  `sd, book` = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, 369.93),
  `99%` = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, quantile(cover$net, 0.99)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
gt(tower, rowname_col = "view") |>
  fmt_number(columns = "mean", rows = c(1, 4, 5), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = "mean", rows = 2:3, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = "mean, book", decimals = 2, drop_trailing_zeros = TRUE) |>
  fmt_number(columns = "sd", rows = 2:3, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = "sd", rows = 5, decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = "sd, book", decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = "99%", decimals = 1) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "") |>
  tab_header("The Book, gross to net", "Per occurrence; claim units")
```

```text
                      mean  mean, book       sd  sd, book      99%
gross               952.70       952.7
half of 300 xs 200  88.497              100.878
500 xs 500          73.019              168.066
ceded, both layers  161.52      161.52
net                 791.18      791.18   369.93    369.93  1,816.0
```

The means are exact on the grid. `cover$on_points` says whether every recovery
landed on a grid point. When it is `FALSE`, the shapes can smear by up to one
step while the means stay exact.

An annual cover is an `aggregate_stop_loss()`, applied to the total of the year.
The stop loss of the session attaches at 30,000 on a book that averages 9,814, so
it never pays. An attachment inside the distribution makes the point:

```{r}
year <- compound_distribution(poisson_count(100), book, POINTS, method = "fft")
stop <- tower_on_grid(
  reinsurance_tower(list(aggregate_stop_loss("5,000 xs 10,000", 5000, 10000))),
  poisson_count(100), book, POINTS
)
cat(sprintf("gross mean %.1f, 99%% %.0f\n", mean(year), quantile(year, 0.99)))
cat(sprintf("stop loss pays %.2f on average\n", mean(stop$ceded[[1]])))
cat(sprintf("net mean %.1f, net 99%% %.0f\n", mean(stop$net), quantile(stop$net, 0.99)))
```

```text
gross mean 9813.7, 99% 13949
stop loss pays 558.87 on average
net mean 9254.8, net 99% 10000
```

Per-layer statistics (how often a layer is hit, loss on line, ceded and net
moments by view) and the contract terms are in the Python guides
[What a reinsurance price is](reinsurance-price.md) and
[Experience and exposure rating](experience-and-exposure-rating.md). The R
package has them as `occurrence_layer_statistics()`,
`aggregate_layer_statistics()` and the `with_*()` contract terms.

## 9. The head to head: FFT against Monte Carlo

Simulate the casualty book five times at 20,000 years each and read the 99.9% quantile.
`simulate_events()` draws each year from its own stream of the generator, so the
same seed gives the same years in R, Python and Rust:

```{r}
exact <- quantile(casualty, 0.999)
seeds <- c(4817, 2531, 9026, 311, 7742)
estimates <- vapply(seeds, function(s) {
  quantile(total(simulate_events(poisson_count(250), claim, 20000, s)), 0.999)
}, 0)
runs <- data.frame(
  run = c("FFT", "FFT, book", paste("simulation, seed", seeds)),
  `99.9%` = c(exact, 33169, estimates),
  `against FFT` = c(NA, NA, estimates / exact - 1),
  check.names = FALSE
)
gt(runs, rowname_col = "run") |>
  fmt_number(columns = "99.9%", decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = "against FFT", decimals = 2, force_sign = TRUE) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "") |>
  tab_header("The casualty book's 99.9% quantile", "FFT against 20,000-year simulations")
```

```text
                        99.9%  against FFT
FFT                    33,170
FFT, book              33,169
simulation, seed 4817  33,145       -0.08%
simulation, seed 2531  33,146       -0.07%
simulation, seed 9026  33,214       +0.13%
simulation, seed 311   32,909       -0.79%
simulation, seed 7742  32,882       -0.87%
```

The 1-unit gap to `aggregate`'s FFT is the quantile convention where the
distribution function crosses 0.999 inside a bucket. At a step of 1 it is the
resolution of the answer. Each simulated estimate rests on the twenty largest of
20,000 years, so it moves by a percent or so from run to run. That matters when it sets capital. The FFT value is the same every run. Simulation is still the tool when
events need an order, a date or a sum insured, or when dependence cannot be put
on a grid (see the Python guide
[Aggregate distributions](aggregate-distributions.md)).

## 10. Portfolios, capital and a first price

A `port` in DecL convolves independent units on one grid. In prospicio that is
`capital_portfolio()`: a named list of grids of the same step, convolved by FFT
as independent units (Python: `Portfolio.from_independent`). The book of the
session has a property unit and a casualty unit. A gamma of CV 0.4 mixes the
casualty count:

```
port Book
    agg Property 80 claims 500 xs 0 sev lognorm 50 cv 1.2 poisson
    agg Casualty 20 claims 2000 xs 0 sev lognorm 250 cv 2.0 mixed gamma 0.4
```

`portfolio_assets(port, p)` gives the lower `p` quantile of the total (Python:
`Portfolio.assets(p)`). `natural_price()` with `p` prices at that level:

```{r}
property_unit <- compound_distribution(
  poisson_count(80), limited_severity(lognormal_from_mean_cv(50, 1.2), 500), POINTS,
  method = "fft"
)
casualty_unit <- compound_distribution(
  mixed_poisson_count(20, 0.4), limited_severity(lognormal_from_mean_cv(250, 2.0), 2000), POINTS,
  method = "fft"
)
book_port <- capital_portfolio(list(Property = property_unit, Casualty = casualty_unit))
priced <- natural_price(book_port, distortion("ccoc", 0.10), p = 0.996)
total_row <- priced[priced$unit == "total", ]
stand_alone <- quantile(property_unit, 0.996) + quantile(casualty_unit, 0.996)
cat(sprintf("99.6%% VaR, units alone summed %s (aggregate: 19,989)\n",
            formatC(stand_alone, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")))
cat(sprintf("99.6%% VaR, portfolio         %s (aggregate: 18,137)\n",
            formatC(portfolio_assets(book_port, 0.996), format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")))
```

```text
99.6% VaR, units alone summed 19,989 (aggregate: 19,989)
99.6% VaR, portfolio         18,137 (aggregate: 18,137)
```

The gap is the diversification benefit. The session then asks for a price that
backs capital with the 99.6% VaR and targets a 10% return on it
(`price_pentagon`). The **pentagon** is loss `L`, margin `M`, premium
`P = L + M`, capital `Q` and assets `a = P + Q`, with the ratios between them. A
constant cost of capital of 10% on assets at the 99.6% quantile prices the book
(`distortion("ccoc", 0.10)` above). `pentagon()` completes the identity from
three of its quantities:

```{r}
pg <- pentagon(loss = total_row$loss, assets = total_row$assets, return_on_capital = 0.10)
compare(
  list(
    list("loss L", pg[["loss"]], 8639.7, 1),
    list("margin M", pg[["margin"]], 863.39, 2),
    list("premium P", pg[["premium"]], 9503.1, 1),
    list("capital Q", pg[["capital"]], 8633.9, 1),
    list("assets a", pg[["assets"]], 18137, 0),
    list("loss ratio", pg[["loss_ratio"]], 0.90915, 5),
    list("premium to capital", pg[["premium_to_capital"]], 1.1007, 4)
  ),
  "The pentagon of the book against aggregate 1.2.0",
  "CCoC 10% at the 99.6% quantile; claim units"
)
```

```text
                    prospicio     book
loss L                8,639.7  8,639.7
margin M               863.39   863.39
premium P             9,503.1  9,503.1
capital Q             8,633.9  8,633.9
assets a               18,137   18,137
loss ratio            0.90915  0.90915
premium to capital     1.1007   1.1007
```

`L` is the expected loss **capped at the assets** (limited liability), a little
under the uncapped mean:

```{r}
cat(sprintf("uncapped mean %.1f, capped at assets %.1f\n",
            mean(property_unit) + mean(casualty_unit), total_row$loss))
units <- priced[priced$unit != "total", ]
for (i in seq_len(nrow(units))) {
  cat(sprintf("%-9s loss %8.1f  premium %8.1f  capital %8.1f\n",
              units$unit[i], units$loss[i], units$premium[i], units$capital[i]))
}
```

```text
uncapped mean 8646.1, capped at assets 8639.7
Property  loss   3972.3  premium   3969.3  capital    -30.3
Casualty  loss   4667.4  premium   5533.8  capital   8664.2
```

The natural allocation splits premium and capital between the units. The Python
guide [Risk loads and distortions](risk-loads-and-distortions.md) explains which
distortion to choose and how to allocate. In R, `calibrate_portfolio()`
calibrates a distortion to a quote.

## 11. Everything is an object you can read

The probabilities of a grid are the numeric vector `@probs`, and `natural_price()` returns a `data.frame`, so a table or a `ggplot2` chart is one line away:

```{r}
print(round(casualty@probs[20001:20003], 6)) # losses of 20,000 to 20,002
cat(sprintf("F(20,000) %.6f\n", cdf(casualty, 20000)))
```

```text
[1] 3.2e-05 3.2e-05 3.2e-05
F(20,000) 0.031989
```

`aggregate` prints the same: 0.000032 per unit near 20,000 and `F(20,000)` of
0.031989.

## 12. DecL clauses and their prospicio equivalents

| DecL | What it says | prospicio (R) |
|---|---|---|
| `250 claims` | expected claim count | the count's mean: `poisson_count(250)` |
| `500 loss` | expected loss, count derived | `poisson_count(500 / mean(claim))` on the limited severity's mean |
| `1000 prem at .65 lr` | premium and loss ratio | expected loss `1000 * 0.65`, then as `500 loss` |
| `1000 xs 0` | per-claim limit | `map_grid(grid, function(x) min(x, 1000))$grid` |
| `130 xs 20` | a layer, claims thinned | `map_grid(grid, function(x) min(max(x - 20, 0), 130))$grid` with the full count (section 7) |
| `[10 20 30] claims [100 200 75] xs [0 50 75]` | a limit profile | one limited grid per limit, then `capital_portfolio()` on a list of grids or a weighted `grid_distribution()` |
| `sev lognorm 100 cv 1.5` | severity by mean and CV | `lognormal_from_mean_cv(100, 1.5)`, `gamma_from_mean_cv()` |
| `sev lognorm [50 100] cv [1 2] wts [.5 .5]` | a mixture | a weighted average of grids (section 4), or `mixture_distribution()` for a continuous severity |
| `dsev [1 2 10] [.4 .4 .2]`, `dfreq [1:5]` | discrete outcomes | `grid_distribution(step, probs)`, `discrete_distribution()`, `empirical_count()` |
| `poisson`, `negbin`, `binomial`, `geometric`, `fixed` | count families | `poisson_count()`, `negative_binomial_count()`, `binomial_count()`, `geometric_count()`, `fixed_count()` |
| `mixed gamma 0.4` | mixed Poisson | `mixed_poisson_count(mean, 0.4)`, with `mixing = "inverse_gaussian"` as an option |
| `zt`, `zm .5` | zero-truncated and zero-modified counts | `zero_truncated_count(base)`, `zero_modified_count(base, 0.5)` |
| `occurrence net of 50% po 300 xs 200` | per-claim cover, net | `xol_layer(name, 300, 200, share = 0.5)` in a `reinsurance_tower()`, `tower_on_grid()`, `$net` |
| `aggregate net of 5000 xs 10000` | annual cover | `aggregate_stop_loss(name, 5000, 10000)` |
| `occurrence ceded to tower [10:50:10]` | a tower of layers | a `reinsurance_tower()` of `xol_layer()`s |
| `reinstatements 1 free and 1 at 50%` | reinstatements | `xol_layer(..., reinstatements = 1)`, `reinstatement_rates = c(...)` |
| `swing`, `slide`, `pc`, `corridor`, `deposit`, `rol`, `rate`, `cede` | contract terms | `with_swing_rating()`, `with_sliding_scale()`, `with_profit_commission()`, `with_loss_corridor()`, `with_deposit_premium()`, `with_rate_on_line()`, `with_premium_rate()`, `with_ceding_commission()` |
| `approximate sgamma` | moment-matched aggregate | `moment_approximation(frequency, severity, "shifted_gamma")` |
| `tweedie p mean dispersion` | a Tweedie aggregate | `tweedie()` |
| `port ... agg ... agg ...` | independent units | `capital_portfolio(list(name = grid, ...))` |
| `bivariate`, `clash` | two lines, one count | `fft_bivariate()`, `clash_model()` with `clash_aggregate()` |
| `pnl`, `xpnl` | premium less loss | `pnl_ledger()`, `pnl_book()`, `pnl_program()` |
| `distortion D ph 0.9` | a distortion | `distortion("proportional_hazard", 0.9)`, and `"wang"`, `"ccoc"`, `"tvar"` and others |
| `port.price(p, ROE)`, `price_pentagon` | capital-loaded price | `natural_price(port, distortion, p = ...)`, `pentagon()` |
| `hints{bs=1/64; log2=16}` | the grid | the `step` and `points` arguments, and `compound_auto(..., log2 = 16)` |

## 13. Speed and the grid audit

The R package runs the same Rust code as the Python package, so the Python
guide's timings against `aggregate` apply to R too: a release build ran 1.1 to
2.1 times faster end to end on the workloads of this tour. They were not
measured from R, and CI does not check them.

`compound_auto()` sizes the grid for an unlimited severity. With a limit or a
portfolio, you pick the step and read `aliasing_error` and `tail_mass` (section
6). `audit_grid()` (and `audit_portfolio_grid()`) does the work of `sharpen`. It
builds the compound at your step and at doubled and halved steps, scores each
build by its moment errors against the exact moments, and returns the best sound
cell. It audits the grid that you give it.

`aggregate` 1.2.0 shares a mixing variable across the severity components of one
`Aggregate` (one mixed count on the claim-weighted mixture) and across the two
units of a bivariate. It never shares it across the units of a portfolio, whose
total is the product of their transforms. prospicio supports both: a mixed
Poisson count compounded on a mixture, and `fft_bivariate()` with a mixed count.
`capital_portfolio()` on a list of grids treats units as independent, as the
portfolios of `aggregate` do.

The Python guides below apply to R too.

- [Aggregate distributions](aggregate-distributions.md): sizing grids and the
  failure modes of the engines.
- [What a reinsurance price is](reinsurance-price.md): the contract terms and the
  technical premium.
- [Risk loads and distortions](risk-loads-and-distortions.md): the pentagon and
  the pricing theory behind it.
